Human Evolution continues

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
............thought humans could not evolve further? Not so!

Unique Selling Point:
Brand new research on continued human evolutions

Summary:
There is a generally perception that human have stopped evolving, that evolution for the human species has halted. But this is not the case. Humans are continuing to evolve -- in fact, they’re doing so at a faster rate than they have in at least 250 years. That’s the conclusion of scientists in Australia who found that more and more people now have the median artery in their arms, and more people are now being born without wisdom teeth, among other findings.

Further information:
There is a generally perception that human have stopped evolving, that evolution for the human species has halted. But this is not the case. Humans are continuing to evolve -- in fact, they’re doing so at a faster rate than they have in at least 250 years. That’s the conclusion of scientists in Australia who found that more and more people now have the median artery in their arms, and more people are now being born without wisdom teeth, among other findings. The research was published last month in the Journal of Anatomy. The states that “people born 80 years from now will all carry a median artery if the trend continues.” The study also concludes that human faces are becoming shorter and jaws smaller, resulting in more people being born without wisdom teeth. The research found other changes starting to occur in humans, including additional bones and bone connections in the legs and feet. Such “microevolution” indicates that humans are evolving at “a faster rate than at any point in the past 250 years.”

And there are other indications that humans have been, and are still undergoing evolution:
• The modern Dutch is on average 10 cm taller that the rest of the industrialized world.
• Some human populations’ genes have been adapted to enable them to drink cow’s milk. Many people on earth cannot drink/digest milk.
• Human brains are evolving -- they have been shrinking over the last 30 000 years (from 1500 cm3 to 1350 cm3 and are becoming more efficient. Downside: continued brain evolution could be the cause of schizophrenia.
• 10 000 years ago, there were no people with blue eyes. It is part of recent human evolution.
• 8000 years ago, humans first encountered Malaria and some groups have evolved to be Malaria resistant
So, in the light of all of this the following can also be asked:
• What will human look like in future, given the fact that we can now manipulate genes in one generation that took natural selection thousands of years?
• Natural selection used to drive evolution. Some say “It’s still going to be selection, it’s just artificial selection now. What we do with breeds of dogs, we’ll do with humans.”
• Skin colour will change. Populations in Africa, for example, are rapidly expanding so those genes increase at a higher frequency on a global population level. Areas of light skin colour are reproducing at lower rates. Therefore, scientists predicts, skin colour from a global perspective will get darker.
• Will space travel and living with lower gravity affect human stature in future?
• Will we become taller and thinner to alleviate global warming?
• And what about transhumanism

Evolution is a gradual change to the DNA of a species over many generations. It can occur by natural selection, when certain traits created by genetic mutations help an organism survive or reproduce. Such mutations are thus more likely to be passed on to the next generation, so they increase in frequency in a population. Gradually, these mutations and their associated traits become more common among the whole group.
===========================================================================
Humans are continuing to evolve -- in fact, they’re doing so at a faster rate than they have in at least 250 years.
That’s the conclusion of scientists in Australia who found that more and more people now have the median artery in their arms, and more people are now being born without wisdom teeth, among other findings.
The research was published last month in the Journal of Anatomy.
The once-rare median artery, long considered chiefly an “embryonic structure,” supplements the radial and ulnar arteries, increasing overall blood flow to the forearm and hand. Flinders University anatomy professor Teghan Lucas and University of Adelaide medical-sciences professors Maciej Henneberg and Jaliya Kumaratilake say their work shows that the median artery will be found in most humans by the end of the century.
“Since the 18th century, anatomists have been studying the prevalence of this artery in adults, and our study shows it’s clearly increasing,” Lucas said in a statement via Flinders University in Adelaide. “The prevalence was around 10% in people born in the mid-1880s compared to 30% in those born in the late 20th century, so that’s a significant increase in a fairly short period of time, when it comes to evolution.”
The Journal of Anatomy study states that “people born 80 years from now will all carry a median artery if the trend continues. When the median artery prevalence reaches 50% or more, it should not be considered as a variant, but as a ‘normal’ human structure.”
The study also concludes that human faces are becoming shorter and jaws smaller, resulting in more people being born without wisdom teeth.
The research found other changes starting to occur in humans, including additional bones and bone connections in the legs and feet.
Lucas says such “microevolution” indicates that humans are evolving at “a faster rate than at any point in the past 250 years.”
++++++++++++++++++++++++++
Scientists have long been fascinated by the sheer tallness of the Dutch, who gained over eight inches in height over the past century and a half. In their search for the secret of that impressive stature, they’ve floated many theories: environmental causes, perhaps, or economics. But a new study suggests that evolution made the Dutch taller than the rest of us.
When a group of behavioral biologists looked at a database of nearly 100,000 Dutch people, they decided to focus on people over the age of 45 who were born (or grown) in the Netherlands to Dutch parents. The sample that remained (about 42,000 people) shared a surprising characteristic: more children per taller man. And taller men were less likely to be childless or single.
This could be evolution in action, the study’s authors suggest. Combined with evidence that taller men tend to have higher incomes, better health and higher ratings from potential sex partners, the new study seems to confirm that sexual selection is alive and well within the Dutch population.

Prof Marciej Henneberg -- world expert in continuing human evolution

Dr Teghan Lucas from Flinders University, the lead investigator in the study

Prof Maryna Steyn, Head of the Department of Anatomy, Wits

Script:


V/O:
Most people think evolution is something that happened, and ended, millions of years ago and that modern humans are exempt from further evolutionary development.

LINK:
But this is not so. Scientists have known for a long time that evolution has not stopped and that it is an ongoing process – even in modern humans.

V/O:
Professor Maryna Steyn, Head of the Department of Anatomy at Wits says she frequently observes new anatomical variations in the human body caused by continuing evolution.

Maryna:
So, indeed, human evolution is still continuing. I think we all know about the example of boys being taller than their dads, and it is a great example of continuing human evolution is the fact that people are getting taller. So, all around us evolution is still happening, and we are adapting to the world around us continuously.
V/O:
The adaptations are small changes in human anatomy.

This is also known as micro-evolution because it takes place within one species, over a relatively short period.

Macro evolution is evolution across species and takes millions of years.

Continuing human micro-evolution made headlines in October when an article in the Journal of Anatomy attracted a lot of media attention. It dealt with the existence of an unexpected median artery in the forearms of adults. Prof Marciej Henneberg a world leader in anatomical evolution at the University of Adelaide was a co-author.
Henneberg:
Median artery is present in each and every human embryo at about six weeks of pregnancy, so very early. It is a normal major artery, and then as the foetus continues developing, the artery disappears and is replaced by the ulnar and radial arteries.

V/O:
However, when dissecting hundreds of cadavers, they found in an increasing number of adults that the median artery has not disappeared. In 1910 only 14% of people had this artery, but now 33% of people have it.

Dr Teghan Lucas of Flinders University co-authored the article.

Teghan:
And yes, it does increase over time and we have beautiful trends that show that. And given our calculations we predict that withing in the next one hundred years approximately upwards of 98% of people are going to have a median artery, so it is happening very quickly.
V/O:
The reason for this evolutionary development is not fully understood, but the team suspects it has something to do with accelerated embryonic development.

Evolutionary changes enable species to adapt better to their environment. For examples, giraffes evolved long necks to enable them to survive on the African savannah. And when humans ventured into colder climates, they evolved lighter skin to adapt to, and survive in an environment with less intense sunlight.

And continuing micro-evolution is causing modern day humans some discomfort. Venessa Stander of Pretoria started to experience pain in her jaw when her wisdom teeth started to erupt.
Vanessa:
I went to the dentist, made an appointment, we had some X-Rays done and I was referred to a specialist. With that we decided that it would be better for me to have my wisdom teeth removed instead of running into complications as year or two down the line.
V/O:
There was just not enough room in Vanessa’s jaw for the erupting teeth, and they had to be removed with a painful surgical procedure.
Vanessa:
So I was put under, my jaw was dislocated and they were removed.
V/O:
Millions of people across the world also experience similar wisdom teeth difficulties. It is the result of continuing human evolution.

Dr Lucas says that unlike our hominid ancestors who had huge jaws, we modern humans do not require such big jaws any longer.
Teghan:
We have fire, we have cutlery we have all there processing techniques, so we don’t chew as much and because of that our faces are getting flatter and we no longer have room in our mandible and maxilla to actually grow our wisdom teeth.
V/O:
And more and more people are nowadays being born without wisdom altogether. It’s evolution’s solution to shrinking jaws that came about because of more efficient food processing.
V/O:
Continuing evolution has also assisted the Inuit to adapt their metabolism to cope with extreme quantities of fat in their diet. This evolutionary adaptation made it possible for them to survive in the arctic with the available food sources.

And about 8000 years ago when humans domesticated cattle, sheep and goats and started to milk them, some groups developed the ability to digest milk as adults, which gave them an evolutionary advantage. It provided them with an additional source of protein.
Link:
Evolution can be extremely beneficial, but sometimes the changes can have negative consequences down the line.
Maryna:
Many, many years ago in west Africa where African sleeping sickness was a huge problem, people developed this specific gene, which provided them with some protection against the disease. And then what happened is that with the slave raids many people in West Africa were transported to the USA, where it was noted that the black population suffer more from chronic kidney disease than other people. And so, all of this was related back to West Africa, the origin of this group where this APL1 gene has evolved. So, while this provides you with protection against sleeping sickness, now to have it in a modern world, is not to your advantage.
V/O:
This is because the refined Western diet of current day America triggers chronic kidney disease in these individuals. Literally dozens of examples of continuing micro evolution in modern humans have been recorded.
Teghan:
Extra bones in the feet, let me clarify, extra bony joints in the feet, so many people could be born with extra joint surfaces. There are people being born with an extra bone in the back of the knee called a fabella. So, what we are seeing now is an increase in these anatomical variations.
V/O:
The reason for some small micro-evolutionary changes are not always immediately evident and will only become clear in future. But they are happening.
LINK:
If humans are continuing to evolve, what are the predictions for us going into the future?
Teghan:
In different global trends I would say on average we will probably be taller, we will probably have much flatter faces, eventually, we will all be born without wisdom teeth, we all probably have a median artery, we will see much more variation body size and shape. Little things will evolve.

Question:
And prof Steyn, how important is it then to be studying micro-evolution. What does it mean for the human race.?

Maryna:
I think it is extremely important to study it because it tells us where we are going. It tells us what we can expect from the future, It also helps us to better understand disease and health, and it also tells us more about us as humans and how adaptable we are to the world that we are living in.

It is part of recent human evolution. • 8000 years ago, humans first encountered Malaria and some groups have evolved to be Malaria resistant So, in the light of all of this the following can also be asked: • What will human look like in future, given the fact that we can now manipulate genes in one generation that took natural selection thousands of years? • Natural selection used to drive evolution. Some say “It’s still going to be selection, it’s just artificial selection now. What we do with breeds of dogs, we’ll do with humans.” • Skin colour will change. Populations in Africa, for example, are rapidly expanding so those genes increase at a higher frequency on a global population level. Areas of light skin colour are reproducing at lower rates. Therefore, scientists predicts, skin colour from a global perspective will get darker. • Will space travel and living with lower gravity affect human stature in future? • Will we become taller and thinner to alleviate global warming? • And what about transhumanism Evolution is a gradual change to the DNA of a species over many generations. It can occur by natural selection, when certain traits created by genetic mutations help an organism survive or reproduce. Such mutations are thus more likely to be passed on to the next generation, so they increase in frequency in a population. Gradually, these mutations and their associated traits become more common among the whole group. =========================================================================== Humans are continuing to evolve -- in fact, they’re doing so at a faster rate than they have in at least 250 years. That’s the conclusion of scientists in Australia who found that more and more people now have the median artery in their arms, and more people are now being born without wisdom teeth, among other findings. The research was published last month in the Journal of Anatomy. The once-rare median artery, long considered chiefly an “embryonic structure,” supplements the radial and ulnar arteries, increasing overall blood flow to the forearm and hand. Flinders University anatomy professor Teghan Lucas and University of Adelaide medical-sciences professors Maciej Henneberg and Jaliya Kumaratilake say their work shows that the median artery will be found in most humans by the end of the century. “Since the 18th century, anatomists have been studying the prevalence of this artery in adults, and our study shows it’s clearly increasing,” Lucas said in a statement via Flinders University in Adelaide. “The prevalence was around 10% in people born in the mid-1880s compared to 30% in those born in the late 20th century, so that’s a significant increase in a fairly short period of time, when it comes to evolution.” The Journal of Anatomy study states that “people born 80 years from now will all carry a median artery if the trend continues. When the median artery prevalence reaches 50% or more, it should not be considered as a variant, but as a ‘normal’ human structure.” The study also concludes that human faces are becoming shorter and jaws smaller, resulting in more people being born without wisdom teeth. The research found other changes starting to occur in humans, including additional bones and bone connections in the legs and feet. Lucas says such “microevolution” indicates that humans are evolving at “a faster rate than at any point in the past 250 years.” ++++++++++++++++++++++++++ Scientists have long been fascinated by the sheer tallness of the Dutch, who gained over eight inches in height over the past century and a half. In their search for the secret of that impressive stature, they’ve floated many theories: environmental causes, perhaps, or economics. But a new study suggests that evolution made the Dutch taller than the rest of us. When a group of behavioral biologists looked at a database of nearly 100,000 Dutch people, they decided to focus on people over the age of 45 who were born (or grown) in the Netherlands to Dutch parents. The sample that remained (about 42,000 people) shared a surprising characteristic: more children per taller man. And taller men were less likely to be childless or single. This could be evolution in action, the study’s authors suggest. Combined with evidence that taller men tend to have higher incomes, better health and higher ratings from potential sex partners, the new study seems to confirm that sexual selection is alive and well within the Dutch population. Interviewees: Prof Marciej Henneberg -- world expert in continuing human evolution Dr Teghan Lucas from Flinders University, the lead investigator in the study An adult individual with a wisdom teeth problem Prof Maryna Steyn, Head of the Department of Anatomy, Wits
